name: Washington

events.title: Statehood
events.text: Washington became the 42nd state on November 11, 1889. Congress gave it 1 seat in the House until the next apportionment.

events.title: 1890 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1890 census, Washington's House delegation grew from 1 to 2 seats.

events.title: Statewide (general ticket) elections
events.text: In the 53rd through 60th Congresses (1893–1909), Washington elected all of its representatives statewide on a general ticket instead of by district.

events.title: 1900 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1900 census, Washington's House delegation grew from 2 to 3 seats.

events.title: 1910 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1910 census, Washington's House delegation grew from 3 to 5 seats.

events.title: Some members elected at-large
events.text: In the 63rd Congress (1913–1915), Washington elected 2 of its representatives statewide (at-large) and the rest by district.

events.title: 1930 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1930 census, Washington's House delegation grew from 5 to 6 seats.

events.title: 1940 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1940 census, Washington kept 6 seats in the House.

events.title: 1950 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1950 census, Washington's House delegation grew from 6 to 7 seats.

events.title: Some members elected at-large
events.text: In the 83rd through 85th Congresses (1953–1959), Washington elected one of its representatives statewide (at-large) and the rest by district.

events.title: 1960 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1960 census, Washington kept 7 seats in the House.

events.title: 1970 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1970 census, Washington kept 7 seats in the House. Because districts must have nearly equal populations, the map was redrawn with the new census counts.

events.title: 1980 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1980 census, Washington's House delegation grew from 7 to 8 seats. Because districts must have nearly equal populations, the map was redrawn with the new census counts.

events.title: Voters create redistricting commission
events.text: On November 8, 1983, voters approved a constitutional amendment giving congressional and legislative redistricting to a commission. Four legislative-leader appointees vote, a nonvoting chair presides, and three votes are needed to adopt a plan.

events.title: Court voids 1982 map; temporary panel redraws
events.text: In Doph v. Munro, a three-judge federal court struck down the legislature's 1982 congressional plan over population differences between districts. In 1983 a temporary bipartisan citizen panel drew a replacement, which the legislature adopted.

events.title: 1990 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1990 census, Washington's House delegation grew from 8 to 9 seats. Because districts must have nearly equal populations, the map was redrawn with the new census counts.

events.title: 2000 census apportionment
events.text: After the 2000 census, Washington kept 9 seats in the House. Because districts must have nearly equal populations, the map was redrawn with the new census counts.

events.title: 2010 census apportionment
events.text: After the 2010 census, Washington's House delegation grew from 9 to 10 seats. Because districts must have nearly equal populations, the map was redrawn with the new census counts.

events.title: Commission misses deadline; court accepts maps
events.text: The commission voted on maps on November 15, 2021, but finished transmitting them after the midnight deadline. On December 3, 2021, the state supreme court found it had substantially complied and let the maps stand; the legislature made minor changes in February 2022.

events.title: 2020 census apportionment
events.text: After the 2020 census, Washington kept 10 seats in the House. Because districts must have nearly equal populations, the map was redrawn with the new census counts.

compactnessNote: Polsby-Popper compactness (4π × area ÷ perimeter²) measured on the projected district shapes. It describes shape only: coastlines, rivers and county lines lower it too, so a low score is not evidence of intent. "Irregular" marks the least compact 5% of district shapes in each census era nationally.

c061.text: Washington's district lines were redrawn between censuses, first used in the 1908 election. The reason has not been researched yet.

c064.text: New map drawn after the 1910 census, which raised Washington's seats from 3 to 5. It was first used in the 1914 election.

c073.text: New map drawn after the 1930 census, which raised Washington's seats from 5 to 6. It was first used in the 1932 election.

c083.text: After the 1950 census raised Washington's seats from 6 to 7, the state kept its existing districts and elected one member statewide (at-large).

c086.text: Washington's district lines were redrawn between censuses, first used in the 1958 election. The reason has not been researched yet.

c087.text: Washington's district lines were redrawn between censuses, first used in the 1960 election. The reason has not been researched yet.

c091.text: Washington's district lines were redrawn between censuses, first used in the 1968 election. The reason has not been researched yet.

c093.text: New map drawn after the 1970 census, which left Washington with 7 seats. It was first used in the 1972 election.

c098.text: New map drawn after the 1980 census, which raised Washington's seats from 7 to 8. It was first used in the 1982 election.

c099.text: New map following: Court voids 1982 map; temporary panel redraws. In Doph v. Munro, a three-judge federal court struck down the legislature's 1982 congressional plan over population differences between districts. In 1983 a temporary bipartisan citizen panel drew a replacement, which the legislature adopted.

c103.text: New map drawn after the 1990 census, which raised Washington's seats from 8 to 9. It was first used in the 1992 election.

c108.text: New map drawn after the 2000 census, which left Washington with 9 seats. It was first used in the 2002 election.

c113.text: New map drawn after the 2010 census, which raised Washington's seats from 9 to 10. It was first used in the 2012 election.

c115.text: Washington's district lines were redrawn between censuses, first used in the 2016 election. The reason has not been researched yet.

c118.text: New map following: Commission misses deadline; court accepts maps. The commission voted on maps on November 15, 2021, but finished transmitting them after the midnight deadline. On December 3, 2021, the state supreme court found it had substantially complied and let the maps stand; the legislature made minor changes in February 2022.
